name: Samara
lede: Samara is a dark bluish green from Maerz and Paul's color dictionary; our books say nothing about it, and the one book hit is an artist's first name.

sections.title: A dictionary name
sections.body: Maerz and Paul recorded Samara in 1922 and published it in their 1930 dictionary, and ISCC-NBS later filed it as a dark bluish green [2]. The origin of the word is undocumented in our sources, so we give none [2]. Related colors are [[green]], [[teal]], [[pine-green]] and [[hooker-s-green]] [2].

sections.title: What the books say
sections.body: Nothing about the color. The only book hit is a caption naming the Australian artist Samara Adamson-Pinczweski, quoted on iridescent paint [1]. That is a person's name, not the color, so we leave it out of the history [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In the archive it appears in 0.75% of paintings (179), as photographed [3]. Most often it is a hidden color in the painting, and it peaks in the 1900s at 2.7 times the expected rate [3]. Renoir is its most devoted painter here, in 5 of 50 works [3]. It is most over-represented in French paintings [3].

notes.cite: ColorHub library, Samara: Maerz & Paul 1930, plate 30 L 5; ISCC-NBS

questions.q: Which painter is most devoted to Samara in our archive?
True or false: our books explain where the color name Samara comes from.
